column4: When Zechariah asks how the promised boy can come, his Rabb answers that it is easy for Him and recalls creating Zechariah from nothing; divine ease directly answers apparent reproductive impossibility.

Mary's corresponding birth question receives the answer that it is easy for her Rabb, who will make the child a sign and mercy; this is a nonlexical but explicit promise of ease immediately before she carries him in 19:22.
Mary asks her Rabb how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and the answer places the otherwise impossible birth under God's unrestricted creating and command.
Before recounting Moses' infancy, God says that He had already favored him another time; this divine reminder of nurturing favor is the direct counterpart to Pharaoh's self-serving reminder in 26:18.
The one who carries wrongdoing fails before the Living, Sustaining One; moral wrong is again made a carried load, with divine sustaining power as its setting.
God says He carried their offspring in the laden ship, joining descendants, divine carrying, and a vessel already bearing a load in one rescue image.
God honors the children of Adam, carries them on land and sea, and provides good things; carrying and provision become acts of continuing divine care for those once carried in wombs.
God recalls that when the water overflowed, “We carried you” in the vessel so the rescue would become a remembrance; divine carrying leads to survival and remembered care.
The girl accepted and grown in 3:36–37 is later told that God chose and purified her above the women of the worlds, a decisive reversal of the inherited shame attached to a female birth.
People count their submission as a favor to the Prophet, but God says that guidance is His favor to them; this distinguishes reproachful human favor-claiming from a truthful divine reminder of care.
Whoever does righteous deeds, male or female, while believing enters the Garden without injustice; divine acceptance is explicitly independent of the sex privileged by the old birth formula.
In the same surah that depicts shame at a daughter's announcement, God promises a good life and full reward to any believing doer of good, male or female.
The believer promises entry into the Garden to every believing righteous person, male or female, replacing valuation by sex with valuation by faith and action.
Pharaoh orders the sons of those who believe with Moses killed and their women spared, another direct exposure of the violent regime behind his claim to have raised one boy.
The trumpet day is called a difficult day; its unrelieved eschatological hardship sets up the explicit denial of ease in 74:10, unlike the section's promise of ease with hardship.
The difficult day is “not easy” for the disbelievers, providing a precise boundary case where hardship is not accompanied by the ease promised to the addressed believer in the section.
Believers are told not to nullify charity by reproachful reminders and injury; this names what is wrong with Pharaoh's use of remembered upbringing as leverage.
The family of Imran is introduced as offspring, one from another, just before the pregnant woman's vow; the birth scene thus belongs to a continuing but divinely heard lineage.
The angels give Mary news of a child identified as the Messiah, initiating the promised-birth scene whose human impossibility she voices in 3:47.
The promised child will speak in the cradle and in maturity, placing infancy and completed growth side by side within Mary's announcement scene.
Mary asks how she can have a boy when no man has touched her and she has not been unchaste; her stated obstacle gives 19:21's declaration of divine ease its concrete birth context.
Mary guards her chastity, receives the breathed spirit, and confirms her Rabb's words; this compressed conception scene supplies the hidden beginning of the child later carried and born.
The parallel account says God breathed into the woman who guarded her chastity and made her and her son a sign, presenting mother and born child together under divine agency.
God makes Mary's son and his mother a sign and shelters them on secure high ground with rest and flowing water, extending the birth image into protective lodging and provision.
God recalls inspiring Moses' mother, making maternal action itself part of the hidden divine nurture elaborated in 20:39–40.
After losing the infant, Moses' mother's heart becomes empty and God strengthens it so she can remain faithful; maternal distress is held and made firm within the caregiving sequence.
Moses' mother sends his sister to follow him, supplying the family care that leads to the nursing solution in 28:12.
When Joseph reaches maturity, God gives him judgment and knowledge; the child whom a household considered adopting in 12:21 is shown brought to full capability.
God creates from weakness, brings strength after weakness, then weakness and gray hair after strength; the life cycle makes gradual formation and decline explicit.
Immediately after the livestock milk and benefits of 23:21, people are carried on the animals and on ships; nourishment and burden-bearing are consecutive provisions.
The donkey carrying books supplies a different kind of load: physical carriage without receiving or living the knowledge borne, sharpening the distinction between carrying and inward appropriation.
The oath invokes bearers carrying a load; although the bearers' identification is interpretively disputed, the ayah contributes the exact act of carrying weight before 51:3 invokes ease.
The next oath invokes those moving with ease, placing easy motion directly after load-bearing without specifying childbirth; the juxtaposition is a cautious indirect parallel to the section.
Giving and God-consciousness are the first conditions preceding facilitation toward ease in 92:7, showing what that ease answers in its own passage.
Affirming the best completes the positive stance before 92:7's promise, locating ease in moral response rather than in the sex of a birth.
Miserliness and self-sufficiency begin the contrary stance that culminates in facilitation toward hardship in 92:10.
Denying the best completes the negative stance before 92:10, clarifying that its hardship answers refusal rather than bodily childbirth.
God reminds people that He created cattle for them, supplying the herds to which the drinks and benefits of 36:73 belong.
The cattle are made manageable, with some serving as mounts and some as food; this gives the human use and control immediately before the herd's drinks are named.
God makes livestock for riding and eating, identifying the animals referred to when 40:80 adds benefits and being carried on them.
Livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food, a broad but concrete picture of the useful abundance behind the section's milk-rich, fruitful flock sense.
Those who spend without following their gift by reproachful reminder or injury retain their reward; this supplies the positive boundary against Pharaoh's weaponized recollection of care.
